questions.prompt: Using a human lifetime as the yardstick, sort each resource as renewable or nonrenewable.
questions.accessiblePrompt: Using a human lifetime as the yardstick, put each resource into one of two groups. Renewable means natural processes replace it within about a human lifetime. Nonrenewable means it takes far longer than a lifetime to form. The resources are: water in lakes and rivers; petroleum, also called crude oil; copper ore; heat from Earth's interior used by geothermal power plants; and fertile topsoil.

bins.label: Renewable: nature replaces it within a human lifetime
Nonrenewable: takes far longer than a human lifetime to form

items.text: Water in lakes and rivers
items.rationale: Rain and snow refill lakes and rivers through the water cycle within months to years, so this water counts as renewable.

items.text: Heat from Earth's interior used by geothermal plants
items.rationale: Heat keeps flowing up from Earth's hot interior, and the cooled water is sent back underground, so geothermal energy is renewable.

items.text: Petroleum (crude oil)
items.rationale: Oil forms from buried sea life over millions of years, far slower than people pump it, so it is nonrenewable.

items.text: Copper ore
items.rationale: Copper ore deposits take millions of years to form, so mining uses them up much faster than nature makes more.

items.text: Fertile topsoil
items.rationale: Building even one centimeter of fertile topsoil can take centuries, and up to a thousand years, while erosion from overgrazing or poor farming can strip it away far faster, so on a human timescale it is nonrenewable.

questions.explanation: Renewable or nonrenewable comes down to how long nature needs to replace a resource. Rain and snow refill lakes and rivers, and Earth's interior keeps supplying heat, both well within a lifetime. Petroleum and copper ore take millions of years to form, and even one centimeter of fertile topsoil can take centuries. Renewable resources can still run short if people use them faster than they are replaced.
questions.misconception: Anything that comes from nature, or from living things, must be renewable.
questions.hint: For each one, ask whether nature could rebuild a used-up supply within one person's lifetime.
questions.limitations: Groundwater is left out on purpose, because aquifers refill on very different timescales: an aquifer under a rainy region can refill quickly, while a deep one under a desert may hold water that soaked in more than a million years ago. Wood is left out because it depends on the kind of forest. Even renewable items can run short if they are overused.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a renewable resource?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Which statement best describes a renewable resource?

choices.text: Nature replaces it within about a human lifetime.
choices.rationale: Correct. Renewable resources are refilled or regrown on a human timescale, so they can last if people do not use them faster than they are replaced.

choices.text: It refills instantly, as soon as people use some of it.
choices.rationale: Renewable resources refill over time, not instantly. A lake drawn down in a drought needs seasons of rain and snow, and a cut forest needs years to regrow.

choices.text: It was made by living things, such as plants or sea life.
choices.rationale: Petroleum was made from living things, yet it is nonrenewable because it takes millions of years to form.

choices.text: It is found on Earth's surface, not deep underground.
choices.rationale: Location is not the test. Geothermal heat comes from underground and is renewable, while fertile topsoil lies at the surface and is nonrenewable.

questions.explanation: A resource is renewable when natural processes can replace it within about a human lifetime. That makes it refillable, not instant or limitless. If people take a lake's water or a geothermal reservoir's steam faster than nature refills it, that use is no longer sustainable and the local supply can run short, even though the resource is still renewable.
questions.misconception: A renewable resource is unlimited or refills instantly.
questions.hint: Lake water and petroleum both come from nature. What makes one renewable and the other not?

questions.prompt: Two companies sell lumber. One harvests a pine plantation every 15 to 20 years and replants each time. The other cuts an old-growth forest of trees several centuries old. Which supply is renewable as it is being managed?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Two companies sell lumber. The first harvests a pine plantation every 15 to 20 years and replants it each time. The second cuts an old-growth forest made of trees that are several centuries old. Which lumber supply is renewable, the way it is being managed?

choices.text: The pine plantation, because regrowth keeps up with the cutting
choices.rationale: Correct. New pines are ready again within a couple of decades, so harvesting and regrowth stay in balance.

choices.text: The old-growth forest, because its huge trees hold far more wood
choices.rationale: A bigger supply is not the same as a renewable one. Trees that took centuries to grow cannot be replaced within many human lifetimes.

choices.text: Both, because trees are living things that can always grow back
choices.rationale: Trees regrow, but wood counts as renewable only when regrowth keeps pace with harvesting. Centuries-old forest cannot be replaced on a human timescale.

choices.text: Neither, because cutting down any tree uses up wood for good
choices.rationale: A replanted plantation grows back within decades, so cutting it does not use up the supply for good.

questions.explanation: Whether wood is renewable depends on how fast it is cut compared with how fast it grows back, not on whether trees are alive. A replanted pine plantation is ready to harvest again in a couple of decades. A forest of centuries-old trees cannot be replaced within many human lifetimes, so cutting it uses up the supply faster than nature restores it.
questions.misconception: All wood is renewable simply because trees are living things that grow back.
questions.hint: Compare how long each forest takes to grow back with how often it is cut.
questions.limitations: Simplified: real forestry also depends on soil, climate and how much of a forest is cut at once. The point is the regrowth time, not the tree species.

evidence.supports: Pine can be harvested about 15 years after planting, while some trees take hundreds of years to grow, so some wood is renewable and some is not, depending on the forest type and the harvest rate.

evidence.supports: Only about 4 percent of the original old-growth coast redwood forest remains, and some living redwoods are about 2,000 years old, so old growth cannot be replaced on a human timescale even though redwoods can resprout.

questions.prompt: Copper ore is nonrenewable, yet recycling has become a major source of copper for new products. How does recycling old copper wire help?

choices.text: It reuses copper that was already mined, so less new ore is dug up.
choices.rationale: Correct. Recycling keeps mined copper in use, which slows how fast ore deposits are emptied, even though it cannot rebuild them.

choices.text: It turns old wire back into ore deposits deep in the crust.
choices.rationale: Recycling happens in factories at the surface. New copper ore forms deep in the crust, mostly from hot fluids given off by magma, over millions of years.

choices.text: It changes copper ore from a nonrenewable resource into a renewable one.
choices.rationale: Ore in the ground still takes millions of years to form, so it stays nonrenewable. Recycling stretches the supply; it does not change how fast nature makes ore.

choices.text: It makes brand-new copper atoms, so Earth's total supply of copper grows.
choices.rationale: Recycling reuses existing copper atoms; it cannot create new ones.

questions.explanation: Recycling cannot make new ore. Ore deposits still take millions of years to form, so copper ore stays nonrenewable. What recycling does is keep already-mined copper in use, so fewer deposits must be mined and the remaining ore lasts longer.

questions.prompt: Shrink all of Earth's water down to 1,000 liters. Using the textbook's rounded values in the table, how many liters would be fresh groundwater?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Imagine all of Earth's water shrunk down to 1,000 liters. A table gives the textbook's rounded values: 97 percent of all water is salt water and 3 percent is fresh. Of that fresh water, 69 percent is ice, 30 percent is groundwater, and 1 percent is in lakes and rivers. How many liters would be fresh groundwater?
questions.workedSolution: Fresh water = 3% of 1,000 L = 0.03 × 1,000 L = 30 L. Fresh groundwater = 30% of that fresh water = 0.30 × 30 L = 9 L. (For comparison, lakes and rivers would be 1% of 30 L = 0.3 L.)
questions.explanation: Fresh water is only a small slice of Earth's water, and most of that slice is frozen. Groundwater makes up most of the rest, which is why aquifers matter so much to farms and cities, while lakes and rivers hold only a sliver.
questions.misconception: Because so much of Earth is covered with water, fresh water that people can use must be plentiful.
questions.hint: First find the fresh water, then take a percentage of that, not of the whole 1,000 liters.
questions.conditions: Uses the textbook's rounded percentages. USGS estimates fresh water at about 2.5 percent of Earth's water, which would give about 7.5 liters of fresh groundwater.
questions.limitations: A scaled-down model of global totals. It says nothing about how evenly that groundwater is spread or how much can be reached.

questions.prompt: An aquifer is underground rock that holds water. Which factors affect how quickly rain and melting snow can refill an aquifer? Select all that apply.
questions.accessiblePrompt: An aquifer is a layer of underground rock that holds water. Which factors affect how quickly rain and melting snow can refill an aquifer? Select all that apply.

choices.text: How much rain and snow falls where water can soak down into it
choices.rationale: Correct. More precipitation where water can soak in means more water is available to move down and refill the aquifer.

choices.text: The type of rock, which controls how easily water soaks in
choices.rationale: Correct. Rock properties control how much water can be stored and how quickly it can move in.

choices.text: How deep underground the aquifer lies
choices.rationale: Correct. Water must travel farther, through all the rock layers in between, to reach a deep aquifer, which is one reason deep ones like the Great Artesian Basin refill so slowly.

choices.text: How much water people pump out of it each year
choices.rationale: Pumping changes how fast water leaves the aquifer, not how fast rain and snowmelt refill it. The aquifer shrinks when pumping outpaces refilling.

choices.text: How close the aquifer is to the ocean, since seawater seeps in to top it up
choices.rationale: Fresh-water aquifers are refilled by rain and snowmelt soaking down from the land. Seawater that seeps into a coastal aquifer makes the water salty; it spoils the fresh supply instead of refilling it.

questions.explanation: Refilling depends on how much water arrives from rain and snow, how easily the rock lets it in and stores it, and how far it has to travel to reach the aquifer. Pumping matters too, but it controls how fast water leaves, not how fast nature puts water back. When people pump faster than the aquifer refills, its water level falls.
questions.misconception: Every aquifer refills at the same rate no matter the climate, the rock or how deep it lies, or the ocean tops up fresh groundwater.
questions.hint: Think about where the water comes from and the path it takes to get underground.
questions.limitations: Simplified model: refilling here means natural recharge from rain and snowmelt. Heavy pumping can sometimes pull in extra water from nearby rivers; that is not counted here.

questions.prompt: Why are petroleum and many other natural resources plentiful in some parts of the world but scarce in others?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Why are petroleum and many other natural resources plentiful in some parts of the world but scarce in others?

choices.text: The conditions that form them existed only in certain places, often for millions of years.
choices.rationale: Correct. Each resource needs particular conditions, such as warm, shallow seas for petroleum or sinking plates for copper ore, and those conditions occurred only in some places.

choices.text: Resources were once spread evenly, but only wealthy nations have searched hard enough to find them.
choices.rationale: Searching affects which deposits are known, but it cannot explain why the deposits themselves are concentrated in certain places.

choices.text: Resources form fastest wherever people need them most, so crowded regions end up with the most.
choices.rationale: Resources formed long before people existed, and their locations were set by geology and climate, not by human need.

choices.text: Resources drift around underground at random, so where they end up is mostly a matter of luck.
choices.rationale: Resources are not scattered at random. Their locations follow from the processes that formed them, which is why scientists can predict where to look.

questions.explanation: Every resource has a formation story tied to place. Because those conditions existed only in certain places, the resources are uneven, and human use reshapes the pattern further.
questions.misconception: Natural resources are spread evenly, and differences between places come only from who has searched or mined.
questions.hint: Think about what it took to make petroleum, and whether that could happen everywhere.

evidence.supports: Petroleum reservoirs are distributed unevenly because petroleum formed where warm, shallow seas existed millions of years ago.

evidence.locator: Introduction; Key Science Concept: The Distribution of Natural Resources
evidence.supports: The abundance of each resource depends on natural processes in Earth's systems, and these cause-and-effect relationships produce an uneven distribution across Earth.

Groundwater collects where rain and snowmelt soak into rock that can store water.
Fertile soil forms as weathered rock mixes with decayed plant and animal matter.

right.text: Rain and snowmelt that soaked down into rock able to store water
Hot, metal-rich fluids from magma that cooled in the crust above a sinking plate

questions.explanation: Each resource carries a signature of how it formed. questions.hint: Look for the key ingredient in each description: sea life, heat, magma fluids, rain or decay. One description fits none of the resources.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order in which petroleum forms, from first to last.
questions.accessiblePrompt: Put these steps in the order in which petroleum forms, from first to last. The steps are: deeper burial raises the heat and pressure on the remains; tiny ocean organisms die and sink to the seafloor; the oil fills tiny spaces in rock, forming a reservoir; layer after layer of sediment buries the remains; the remains change chemically into thick, dark oil.

items.text: Deeper burial raises the heat and pressure on the remains
items.rationale: Third: only after the remains are buried deeply do heat and pressure build up.

items.text: Tiny ocean organisms die and sink to the seafloor
items.rationale: First: the raw material is the remains of tiny sea plants and animals settling to the bottom.

items.text: The oil fills tiny spaces in rock, forming a reservoir
items.rationale: Last: the oil that forms collects in the pore spaces of rock, making a reservoir that wells can reach.

items.text: Layer after layer of sediment buries the remains
items.rationale: Second: new sediment piles on top, burying the remains deeper and deeper.

items.text: The remains change chemically into thick, dark oil
items.rationale: Fourth: once heat and pressure are high enough, the remains undergo chemical changes that produce oil.

questions.explanation: Petroleum begins as tiny sea organisms that settle on the seafloor. Sediment buries them deeper and deeper, the heat and pressure rise, and over millions of years the remains change chemically into oil, which collects in the pore spaces of rock. Each step needs the one before it, which is why the whole process takes so long.
questions.misconception: Oil forms on the seafloor before the remains are buried, or heat and pressure act on the remains before they are buried deeply.
questions.hint: Nothing can be cooked by heat and pressure until it has been buried.

evidence.locator: Section 3, Formation and Figure 3A, How Petroleum Forms
evidence.supports: Marine organisms die and settle to the seafloor, are buried under layers of sediment, and over millions of years heat and pressure change them into oil that fills pore spaces in rock.

evidence.title: Oil and petroleum products explained
evidence.supports: EIA describes crude oil forming from ancient marine organisms buried under layers of sand, silt and rock, whose heat and pressure turned the remains into oil found in tiny spaces within sedimentary rocks.

questions.prompt: Rain and snow refill a valley's aquifer by 20 million cubic meters a year. The town pumps 8 million for drinking water, and farms pump 30 million. If the town's share stays the same, what is the most the farms can pump each year so the stored water stops shrinking?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Rain and snow refill a valley's aquifer by 20 million cubic meters of water each year. The town pumps 8 million cubic meters each year for drinking water, and farms pump 30 million cubic meters each year. If the town's share stays the same, what is the most the farms can pump each year, in million cubic meters, so that the stored water stops shrinking?
questions.workedSolution: To stop the stored water from shrinking, total pumping can be at most the refill rate, 20 million m³ per year. The town keeps 8 million, so the farms can pump at most 20 − 8 = 12 million m³ per year, down from 30 million.
questions.explanation: An aquifer works like a savings account: if more goes out than comes in, the balance falls. Matching total pumping to the refill rate keeps the stored water steady, which is the heart of managing a slowly refilled aquifer like Australia's Great Artesian Basin. Here the town's drinking water is set first and the farms get what is left. Deciding who comes first is a choice people make; the refill rate sets the total everyone must share.
questions.misconception: An aquifer is safe as long as some water is still being added each year.
questions.hint: First find the most everyone together can pump, then subtract the town's share.
questions.conditions: Assume the refill rate stays at 20 million cubic meters per year, the town keeps pumping 8 million, and pumping is the only way water leaves.
questions.limitations: Real aquifers also lose water to springs and rivers, and refilling changes from year to year with the weather.

evidence.supports: When people remove groundwater faster than it is replenished, aquifers become depleted; the Great Artesian Basin's use is managed so it can remain a water source.
